title: Mahatma Gandhi and the Indian National Movement: 1917–1947

fiveW.when: Developed in South Africa from 1893; used in India from 1917
fiveW.what: Satyagraha — devotion to truth; non-violent resistance
fiveW.why: Shocked by racial discrimination against non-Whites in South Africa
fiveW.how: Truth and non-violence; fearless resistance to evil; accepting suffering

notes.content:
• Born **2 October 1869, Porbandar (Gujarat)**; studied **law in England**; went to **South Africa (1893)** as a barrister; fought **racial discrimination** there.
• **Satyagraha** = devotion to truth, based on **truth and non-violence**. A satyagrahi is **fearless**, opposes evil, and accepts **sacrifice and suffering**.

**Methods of satyagraha**
• **Peaceful demonstrations**.
• **Defiance of unjust laws**.
• **Boycott** of British goods and services.
• **Non-payment** of oppressive taxes.
• **Swadeshi** — **charkha** and homespun **khadi**.

**Chapter map:** Champaran → Kheda → Ahmedabad → Rowlatt/Jallianwala → Non-cooperation → Simon/Poorna Swaraj → Civil Disobedience → 1935 Act → Cripps → Quit India → INA → Cabinet Mission → Partition → Independence.

fiveW.who: Gandhi with indigo cultivators, Kheda peasants and Ahmedabad mill workers; won over Rajendra Prasad and Vallabhbhai Patel
fiveW.what: First satyagrahas in India — all successful
fiveW.why: Oppression by indigo planters; tax during crop failure; low wages

notes.content:
| Place | Year | For whom | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Champaran** (Bihar) | **1917** — first | **Indigo cultivators** vs European planters | **Rent reduced** |
| **Kheda** (Gujarat) | **1918** | Peasants (crops failed) | **Tax collection suspended** for a year |
| **Ahmedabad** (Gujarat) | **1918** | **Textile mill workers** | **Wages raised** |

Won support of **Dr Rajendra Prasad** (Bihar) and **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** (Gujarat).

**Gandhi's visions**
• **Hindu-Muslim unity** — 'Indian culture… is a fusion of all.'
• **Social justice** — uplift of lower castes, whom he called **Harijans** ('children of God'), and women.
• After returning in **1915**, he toured India and saw that **mass support** was essential → organised peasants and workers.

fiveW.who: General Dyer vs unarmed people of Amritsar
fiveW.why: Protest against the Rowlatt Act; Dyer had banned meetings
fiveW.how: Troops blocked the only exit and fired without warning until ammunition ran out

notes.content:
**Rowlatt Act (March 1919) — the 'Black Act'**
• **Arrest without warrant**.
• Political **trials without jury**.
• **Imprisonment for an indefinite period**.
• **6 April 1919** — Gandhi called for a national **fast, meetings and hartal**.

**Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (13 April 1919)**
• Peaceful, unarmed meeting in **Amritsar** against the Rowlatt Act.
• **General Dyer** blocked the **only exit** and fired **without warning** till ammunition ran out → **hundreds killed, thousands wounded**.
• **Tagore returned his knighthood**; **martial law** in Punjab.
• Gandhi **lost faith in British justice** → non-cooperation.

fiveW.who: Gandhi and the Congress, with the Khilafat leaders (Ali brothers)
fiveW.where: All India; ended after Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur, UP)
fiveW.what: First mass movement — refusal to cooperate with the British
fiveW.why: Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh, Khilafat issue; to win self-government
fiveW.how: Boycott of councils, courts, schools, titles and foreign goods; khadi and charkha

notes.content:
**Methods**
• **Boycott** of legislative councils, **law courts**, government **schools and colleges**, government functions and **elections**.
• **Surrender of titles** and honorary posts.
• **Swadeshi**; boycott of **foreign goods**; **khadi** — **charkha** became the symbol.
• **Hindu-Muslim unity** — supported the **Khilafat Movement** (1919, **Ali brothers — Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali**, against abolition of the Caliph in Turkey).

**Impact:** first **large-scale mass movement**; Congress changed from a 'microscopic minority' into a **mass-based party**; Muslims joined the freedom fight.

**Withdrawal — Chauri Chaura (1922):** police fired on a peaceful procession; the angry mob **burnt the police station**, killing policemen → Gandhi **called off** the movement because of violence.

fiveW.who: Sir John Simon's commission; Congress under Jawaharlal Nehru
fiveW.what: Boycott of the all-White commission; demand for complete independence
fiveW.why: No Indian member on the commission
fiveW.how: 'Simon Go Back' protests; Poorna Swaraj resolution; 26 January 1930 as Independence Day

notes.content:
**Simon Commission (1927)** — headed by **Sir John Simon** to review British rule.
• **Boycotted** because it was an **all-White commission** with **no Indian member**; its recommendations were unacceptable.

**Lahore Session (December 1929)** — President **Jawaharlal Nehru**
• **Poorna Swaraj** (complete independence) resolution adopted.
• Decided to **boycott the First Round Table Conference**.
• **26 January 1930** declared **Independence Day**; **tricolour** unfurled; pledge of freedom.
• Decided to launch **Civil Disobedience** under Gandhi.

**Why 26 January matters today:** our **Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950** — Republic Day.

notes.subtopic: 6. Civil Disobedience Movement and Dandi March (1930–34)

fiveW.who: Gandhi and thousands of followers (including Sarojini Naidu)
fiveW.what: Salt Satyagraha — breaking the salt law
fiveW.why: British monopoly and tax on salt, a necessity for every household
fiveW.how: Marched to Dandi and picked up a handful of salt; salt was then made and sold openly across India

notes.content:
• **Salt law:** British **monopoly** on salt; Indians **taxed** and **not allowed to make it**.
• **March 1930** — **Dandi March** from **Sabarmati Ashram** to **Dandi**; Gandhi picked up a **handful of salt** → symbolic defiance copied all over India.
• **All-India mass movement:** strikes, hartals, boycott of offices, schools, colleges; **refusal to pay taxes**; boycott of foreign goods; truly **non-violent**; large participation of **women**.
• **Repression:** Gandhi, Nehru and thousands **arrested**; lathi-charges and firing.

**Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931)** — Viceroy **Lord Irwin**: Gandhi **suspended** the movement and agreed to attend the **Second Round Table Conference**; Irwin agreed to **release prisoners** and **permit salt-making**.

**Second Round Table Conference (Sept–Dec 1931)** — Gandhi the **sole Congress representative**; nothing on self-rule → returned **empty-handed** → movement **relaunched**.

**Result:** British realised reforms were needed → **Government of India Act 1935**.

notes.subtopic: 7. 1935 Act, World War II and the Cripps Mission
notes.content:
• **Government of India Act, 1935** → **elections in 1937** — **Congress won by a huge margin** (Muslim League also contested).
• **1939 — World War II:** Britain needed Indian support; leaders would help only if India was made **independent** → **deadlock**.

**Cripps Mission (1942)** — **Sir Stafford Cripps**
• **Dominion status after the war**.
• Provinces/princely states could **stay out** of the Indian Dominion.
• **Gandhi rejected it** — a **'post-dated cheque'**; 'too little, too late'; no real transfer of power.

**Comparative history:** the **Great Depression (1929–39)** — worldwide economic slump starting with the US stock market crash.

fiveW.who: Gandhi, Congress and the people of India
fiveW.where: All India; parallel governments at Ballia (UP) and Midnapore (Bengal)
fiveW.what: Final mass movement demanding that the British quit India
fiveW.why: Failure of the Cripps Mission; the British would not transfer real power
fiveW.how: 'Do or Die'; leaders arrested at once; spontaneous protests, strikes, sabotage

notes.content:
• **August 1942** — Congress resolved to launch **Quit India**; Gandhi's slogan **'Do or Die'**.
• **All leaders arrested** before it began; **Congress banned**.

**Features**
• **Spontaneous** marches, demonstrations, strikes without leaders.
• After lathi-charges and firing, people attacked **government buildings, railway and police stations**, **cut telegraph lines**, damaged tracks.
• **Army called out**; thousands killed; movement suppressed.
• **Parallel governments** at **Ballia (UP)** and **Midnapore (Bengal)**.

**Importance:** new **confidence**; demand now **complete independence, not dominion status**; **united** Indians; after the war Britain could no longer ignore the demand.

notes.subtopic: 9. Subhas Chandra Bose and the INA

fiveW.who: Subhas Chandra Bose (Netaji); Captain Mohan Singh
fiveW.where: Calcutta → Berlin → Japan, Singapore; Burma, Kohima, Imphal
fiveW.what: Azad Hind Fauj (Indian National Army) — armed struggle for freedom
fiveW.why: To free India quickly through military action, with Japanese help
fiveW.how: Formed the Forward Bloc; escaped abroad; led the INA and a Provisional Government of Free India

notes.content:
• **Congress President 1938 and 1939**; resigned after differences with Gandhi.
• **Forward Bloc (1939)** — aims: **freedom in the immediate future** and **national unity**.
• Protested India being dragged into the war → **imprisoned**, then under **house arrest** → **escaped to Berlin**, then **Japan**.
• **Sept 1942** — **Captain Mohan Singh** formed the **Azad Hind Fauj (INA)** with **40,000** Indian soldiers.
• **July 1943** — Bose took command; hailed **'Netaji'**; slogan **'Give me blood and I will give you freedom'**.
• **1943** — **Provisional Government of Free India** in **Singapore**; declared war on the Allies.
• **1944** — INA with the Japanese captured **Kohima**, reached **Imphal**, **hoisted the tricolour**; later defeated when the British regained **Burma**.
• **Legacy:** heroic example; INA marching song **'Kadam kadam badhaye ja'** (Vanshidhar Shukla) is still played by the Indian Army.

fiveW.who: Clement Attlee, Cabinet Mission, Nehru, Jinnah, Lord Mountbatten
fiveW.why: Post-war Britain could not hold India; communal violence after Direct Action Day
fiveW.how: Cabinet Mission, Interim Government, Mountbatten Plan, Indian Independence Act 1947

notes.content:
• **1945** — **Labour Party** under **Clement Attlee** came to power in Britain.
• **Cabinet Mission (1946)** — to plan the **transfer of power**.
• **1946** — **Nehru** invited to form the **Interim Government**.
• **16 August 1946** — **Jinnah** launched **Direct Action Day** for Pakistan → **communal violence**.
• **March 1947** — **Lord Mountbatten**, last Viceroy; **Mountbatten Plan** — two dominions, **India and Pakistan**.

**Indian Independence Act (July 1947)**
• Two independent dominions with defined territories.
• A Governor-General for each — **Mountbatten (India)**, **Jinnah (Pakistan)**.
• British responsibility ends **15 August 1947**; **Secretary of State abolished**.

• **15 August 1947** — tricolour at the **Red Fort**; **Nehru first Prime Minister**.
• Gandhi's **fast unto death** to stop communal violence.
• **26 January 1950** — Constitution adopted; India a **sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic**.

questions.question: What is satyagraha? Describe Gandhi's methods of protest.
questions.answer:
• Satyagraha = devotion to truth; resistance to evil through truth and non-violence; a satyagrahi is fearless and accepts suffering.
  • Methods: peaceful demonstrations; defiance of unjust laws; boycott of British goods and services; non-payment of oppressive taxes; swadeshi through the charkha and khadi.

questions.question: Describe Gandhi's early satyagrahas in India.
questions.answer:
• Champaran (1917, Bihar): for indigo cultivators against European planters — rent reduced.
  • Kheda (1918, Gujarat): for peasants whose crops failed — tax suspended for a year.
  • Ahmedabad (1918): for textile mill workers — wages raised.

They won him Rajendra Prasad and Vallabhbhai Patel as supporters.

questions.question: Mention two clauses of the Rowlatt Act.
questions.answer:
• Arrest without warrant.
  • Trial of political cases without jury; imprisonment for an indefinite period.

questions.question: How did the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre lead to the Non-cooperation Movement?
questions.answer:
• On 13 April 1919 General Dyer fired on a peaceful, unarmed meeting against the Rowlatt Act, blocking the only exit — hundreds died.
  • Nationwide protests; Tagore returned his knighthood; martial law in Punjab.
  • Gandhi lost all faith in British justice and urged Indians not to cooperate with such a government.
  • In 1920 he launched the Non-cooperation Movement, joined with the Khilafat Movement to unite Hindus and Muslims.

questions.question: Describe the methods, impact and withdrawal of the Non-cooperation Movement.
questions.answer:
• Methods: boycott of councils, courts, schools, elections and foreign goods; surrender of titles; swadeshi, khadi and the charkha; Hindu-Muslim unity via Khilafat.
  • Impact: first mass movement; Congress became a mass-based party; Muslims joined the freedom struggle.
  • Withdrawal: at Chauri Chaura (1922) a mob burnt a police station killing policemen; Gandhi called off the movement as it had turned violent.
questions.topperTip: Methods → Impact → Withdrawal: three headings, full marks.

questions.question: Why was the Simon Commission boycotted?
questions.answer: The Simon Commission (1927) was an all-White commission — it had no Indian member to represent India, though it was to decide India's future. Its recommendations were also unacceptable to national leaders.

questions.question: What decisions were taken at the Lahore session of 1929?
questions.answer:
• Presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru.
  • Poorna Swaraj (complete independence) adopted as the goal.
  • Boycott of the First Round Table Conference.
  • 26 January 1930 declared Independence Day; tricolour unfurled.
  • Civil Disobedience to be launched under Gandhi.

questions.question: Describe the Civil Disobedience Movement.
questions.answer:
• Cause: Poorna Swaraj resolution; unjust salt law (British monopoly and tax).
  • Dandi March (March 1930): Sabarmati to Dandi; Gandhi picked up salt — salt made across India.
  • Spread: strikes, hartals, boycotts, non-payment of taxes; non-violent; many women took part.
  • Repression: leaders arrested; lathi-charges, firing.
  • Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) → Second Round Table Conference → failed → movement relaunched → Government of India Act 1935.

questions.question: What were the terms of the Gandhi-Irwin Pact?
questions.answer:
• Gandhi: suspend Civil Disobedience; attend the Second Round Table Conference.
  • Irwin: release all prisoners; permit people to make salt.

questions.question: What was the Cripps Mission? Why did Gandhi reject it?
questions.answer:
• Sent in 1942 under Sir Stafford Cripps to win Indian support in World War II.
  • Proposals: dominion status after the war; provinces and princely states could stay out of the Indian Dominion.
  • Gandhi called it a 'post-dated cheque' — too little, too late, with no real transfer of power (and a risk of breaking India into pieces).

questions.question: What were the features and importance of the Quit India Movement?
questions.answer:
• Launched August 1942; slogan 'Do or Die'; leaders arrested at once, Congress banned.
  • Features: spontaneous protests and strikes; attacks on government buildings, railway and police stations; telegraph lines cut; army called out, thousands killed; parallel governments at Ballia and Midnapore.
  • Importance: new confidence; demand for complete independence, not dominion status; united Indians; Britain could no longer ignore the demand after the war.

questions.question: (Picture) Identify the freedom fighter, the party he formed in 1939 and the organisation he led from 1943.
questions.answer:
• (a) Subhas Chandra Bose (Netaji).
  • (b) Forward Bloc.
  • (c) Azad Hind Fauj / Indian National Army (INA).

questions.question: Despite its defeat, did the INA play a significant role in the freedom struggle? Give reasons.
questions.answer:
Yes.

  • Netaji's call — 'Give me blood and I will give you freedom' — inspired Indians everywhere.
  • The INA and the Provisional Government of Free India showed Indians could fight as a free nation; it reached Kohima and Imphal and hoisted the tricolour.
  • It showed the British that the loyalty of Indian soldiers could no longer be taken for granted.
  • Netaji became an icon of patriotism; its song still inspires the Indian Army.

questions.question: Who were the two main Indian leaders in 1946? What happened after Direct Action Day?
questions.answer:
• Jawaharlal Nehru (Congress; invited to form the Interim Government) and Mohammed Ali Jinnah (Muslim League).
  • Jinnah launched Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) to press for Pakistan; it was followed by communal violence all over the country, which made Partition seem the only solution.

questions.question: State the main provisions of the Indian Independence Act, 1947.
questions.answer:
• Two independent dominions — India and Pakistan — with defined territories.
  • A Governor-General for each — Mountbatten for India, Jinnah for Pakistan.
  • British responsibility for India to end on 15 August 1947.
  • The office of the Secretary of State abolished.
